listeningScripts.title: Renting a flat — phone enquiry
listeningScripts.script:
Now you will hear Part 1. You will hear a conversation between a letting agent called Sandra and a man called Tom Webb who is looking for a flat to rent. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

[Pause]

Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

Sandra: Good morning, Riverside Properties. This is Sandra speaking. How can I help you?

Tom: Oh, good morning. My name is Tom Webb. I'm calling about the flat you have advertised in the Gazette. The two-bedroom one on Ashford Road?

Sandra: Yes, of course! That property is still available. Can I just take a few details from you, Mr Webb?

Tom: Certainly.

Sandra: Right. And your first name is Tom, you said?

Tom: Yes, that's right. Tom.

Sandra: Lovely. And could I get your email address, please?

Tom: It's t-webb — that's T hyphen W-E-B-B — at fastmail dot com.

Sandra: T-webb at fastmail dot com. Perfect. And a contact number?

Tom: My mobile is 07851 334 209.

Sandra: Let me just read that back — 07851 334 209?

Tom: Yes, that's correct.

Sandra: Great. Now, the flat is on Ashford Road. Are you familiar with that area at all?

Tom: Yes, actually. I work nearby. I'm a nurse at St Catherine's hospital, which is only a ten-minute walk away. The location really is ideal for me.

Sandra: Oh, that's great to hear. So, are you looking to move in fairly soon?

Tom: Yes, I'd like to move in from the first of March if possible.

Sandra: The first of March. Let me just check... yes, that works perfectly with the end of the current tenancy. So that's all fine.

Tom: Excellent. And the rent was listed as eight hundred and fifty pounds per month?

Sandra: That's right. Eight hundred and fifty a month, unfurnished. The deposit is one month's rent, so another eight hundred and fifty up front.

Tom: I see. Now, is parking included with the flat?

Sandra: Yes, there is one allocated parking space in the rear courtyard, included in the rent. 

Tom: Oh, wonderful. I was worried about that.

[Pause]

Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

[Pause]

Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

Sandra: Now, the flat itself is on the third floor — there's a lift, so that shouldn't be a problem — and it faces south, so it gets a lot of light in the afternoon.

Tom: That sounds lovely. What's included in the property?

Sandra: The kitchen has an integrated oven and dishwasher, and there's a washing machine in the utility cupboard off the hallway. The bathroom has a shower — no bath, just a shower — over the cubicle.

Tom: That's fine. Is the broadband already set up?

Sandra: Broadband isn't connected, but the fibre cables are already installed, so you'd just need to contact a provider and it could be up and running within a week. It's one of the most popular flats we have for that reason — the speed is very good in that building.

Tom: Perfect. And what about bills — are any included?

Sandra: Water rates are included in the rent. Gas, electricity and council tax are the tenant's responsibility.

Tom: Understood. And is the landlord happy with pets? I have a small cat.

Sandra: I'll need to check on that specifically — the landlord hasn't mentioned pets in the listing. I'd say ring me back tomorrow afternoon and I should have an answer.

Tom: Perfect. I'll call you back tomorrow. And is it possible to arrange a viewing?

Sandra: Absolutely. Our next available slot is Thursday the twentieth at two-thirty in the afternoon. Does that suit you?

Tom: Thursday the twentieth at two-thirty — yes, that's perfect.

Sandra: Wonderful. I'll confirm that by email. Thank you, Mr Webb.

Tom: Thank you, Sandra. Goodbye.

Sandra: Goodbye.

That is the end of Part 1.

listeningScripts.title: Community centre activities talk
listeningScripts.script:
Now you will hear Part 2. You will hear a woman called Claire giving a talk about the facilities and programme at the Millbridge Community Centre. First, look at questions 11 to 15.

[Pause]

Hello everyone, and welcome to the Millbridge Community Centre open morning. My name is Claire, and I'm the centre coordinator. We're really delighted you've all come along today to find out more about what we offer.

I'll start by describing the layout of the building. As you came in through the main entrance on Kendal Street, you'll have passed our reception desk on your left. The café is straight ahead at the end of the main corridor — it's open Monday to Saturday, nine to five. To the right of reception, you'll find the sports hall, which is our largest space. It seats up to two hundred people for events or accommodates twelve badminton courts when set up for sport. The fitness suite is upstairs on the first floor, directly above the sports hall.

If you turn left at reception and follow the corridor, you'll pass the children's library on your right — it's a wonderful little room with bean bags and low shelves, very popular with families — and at the end of that corridor, you'll come to the main meeting room, which we hire out for private events. The art studio is further along past the meeting room, in the far corner of the building.

Now, a few important things to note. The car park is behind the building, accessed from Baker Lane, not from Kendal Street. Blue badge spaces are right next to the rear entrance.

[Pause]

Now look at questions 16 to 20.

[Pause]

I'd now like to tell you about some of the activities and courses we run this term. We have something for almost everyone.

Our new beginners' swimming class for adults has been hugely popular. The sessions run on Tuesday and Thursday evenings, from seven to eight o'clock, and they take place at Millbridge Leisure Pool just five minutes' walk from here — not in this building. The cost is eight pounds per session, or forty pounds if you book a block of six.

For those of you interested in creative activities, our pottery class begins on the third of next month. It runs every Saturday morning from ten to twelve. Places are limited to twelve per session, and I'm afraid six are already taken, so please sign up today if you're keen.

We also run a Digital Skills Workshop every Wednesday afternoon at two o'clock, aimed at adults who want to improve their confidence using computers, smartphones, and the internet. This one is completely free of charge, funded by the local council.

Finally, I'd like to mention our Community Choir. This is open to absolutely everyone — no experience or auditions required. It meets on the first and third Monday of each month at seven-thirty in the evening. The choir performs at local events three or four times a year, which members really enjoy.

If any of these activities interest you, please see the booking desk in the lobby before you leave today. Leaflets with full details are also available there.

That is the end of Part 2.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace volunteer project discussion
listeningScripts.script:
Now you will hear Part 3. You will hear two colleagues, Maya and James, discussing a workplace volunteering project. First, look at questions 21 to 25.

[Pause]

Maya: James, have you had a chance to look at the feedback from the community garden project we ran last month?

James: Yes, I went through the survey results this morning. Overall I thought it was quite positive, but some of the comments surprised me.

Maya: Same for me. What stood out for you?

James: Well, I expected people to say the main difficulty was the physical work — digging and lifting, that sort of thing. But actually, the thing most volunteers struggled with was coordinating who was doing what. There was a lot of confusion about tasks on the first day.

Maya: That matches what I read. Several people mentioned arriving and not knowing where to go or what tools to pick up. I think we really underestimated how important a proper briefing is at the start.

James: Exactly. And it wasn't just the volunteers who noticed — a couple of the garden supervisors commented on it too. They felt they spent too much time directing people rather than actually getting on with the work.

Maya: So for the next project, I think we should prepare a printed task list and give everyone a specific role before they arrive.

James: I agree completely. Also, I thought the morning start time worked well, but some people commented they would have preferred a two-hour slot rather than a full day. A few said they struggled to commit to a whole Saturday.

Maya: That's useful to know. Maybe we could offer both options next time — a morning half-day and an afternoon half-day.

James: Good idea. More flexibility would probably get more sign-ups.

[Pause]

Now look at questions 26 to 30.

[Pause]

Maya: What about the location? I thought Riverside Park was a great choice, but some people mentioned the travel was inconvenient.

James: Yes, I saw that. A few volunteers came from the Northside area and said the bus journey was forty minutes each way. That's quite a commitment on top of a full volunteering day.

Maya: I wonder if we should look at projects closer to the office for next time. Or maybe arrange a minibus from the car park?

James: A minibus is a good idea, but it would add to the budget. Let me look at what the transport allowance covers.

Maya: Fair enough. Now, thinking about what went well — the team atmosphere was mentioned by almost everyone as a highlight.

James: Yes, the survey was really strong on that. People liked working alongside colleagues from different departments they don't normally interact with. A couple of people said it actually changed how they felt about their work relationships.

Maya: That's exactly what volunteering projects should do — build internal connections as well as contribute to the community.

James: Agreed. So, for our report to the CSR committee, I'd suggest we recommend continuing the programme, with changes to the briefing process and location options.

Maya: Perfect. I'll draft that section if you want to handle the budget analysis.

James: That works for me.

That is the end of Part 3.

listeningScripts.title: Talk on the history of coffee
listeningScripts.script:
Now you will hear Part 4. You will hear a presenter giving a talk about the history of coffee and its role in global society. First, look at questions 31 to 40.

[Pause]

Good morning. Today I want to talk about something that billions of people engage with every day without giving it a second thought: coffee. It's the world's second most traded commodity after oil, and the story of how a small red berry discovered in the highlands of East Africa came to reshape economies, societies and even political life across the globe is a fascinating one.

The earliest credible accounts of coffee consumption date to the fifteenth century, in the Sufi monasteries of Yemen. Monks found that the drink — made by boiling ground roasted beans in water — helped them to stay alert during long periods of prayer and meditation at night. From Yemen, trade routes carried coffee northward into Mecca and Medina, and from there across the Ottoman Empire. By the mid-sixteenth century, coffeehouses had appeared in Constantinople — which we now call Istanbul — and they became the first genuinely public spaces where men of all social classes could sit, converse, and debate current affairs. These establishments were sometimes called 'schools of the wise', which gives you a sense of the intellectual reputation they acquired.

Coffee's arrival in Europe is usually dated to the 1600s, and the reaction was mixed. Some religious authorities objected, calling it the 'bitter invention of Satan', and Pope Clement VIII was urged to ban it. According to historical accounts, he tasted it first and reportedly enjoyed it so much that he gave it papal approval — though historians debate whether this story is entirely accurate. Regardless, coffeehouses spread rapidly. London alone had over three hundred by 1675, each one becoming a hub for merchants, lawyers, writers and politicians.

What is less often discussed is the darker economic history underpinning the coffee trade. By the eighteenth century, European colonial powers — particularly the Dutch and the French — had transplanted coffee cultivation from Yemen to their colonies in Java, Suriname and the Caribbean. This expansion relied heavily on enslaved labour, and the profits generated contributed significantly to the accumulation of wealth in European countries. The relationship between coffee and colonialism is one that contemporary historians have brought much greater scrutiny to in recent decades.

In terms of consumption patterns, the nineteenth century saw a dramatic shift. Industrial workers in northern European countries began drinking coffee in large quantities because it was an affordable stimulant that helped maintain productivity during long factory shifts. By the early twentieth century, annual global consumption had reached over one million tonnes. Today that figure is closer to ten million tonnes per year.

The modern specialty coffee movement, which emerged in the 1970s in the United States, introduced a new language and culture around origin, roasting profiles and brewing methods. This transformed coffee from a commodity into something more akin to wine — a product associated with connoisseurship, provenance and artisan craft. The rise of the espresso bar in Italy, and later the global expansion of coffee chain culture in the 1990s and 2000s, made coffee drinking a defining feature of urban professional life worldwide.

Today, coffee farming supports over one hundred and twenty-five million livelihoods globally, the majority in developing countries in the so-called 'coffee belt' — the tropical zone between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. Climate change poses a serious threat to this sector: rising temperatures and unpredictable rainfall are already reducing yields in key producing regions such as Ethiopia, Colombia and Vietnam, and researchers estimate that up to fifty per cent of current coffee-growing land could become unsuitable by 2050 if current warming trends continue.

The story of coffee, then, is not simply one of a pleasant morning ritual. It is a story of trade and colonialism, of intellectual life and social gathering, of industrial capitalism and contemporary climate vulnerability. To drink coffee is, in a sense, to participate in a history that spans five centuries and connects people across every continent.

That is the end of Part 4. That is also the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
